speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers; for the administration of the proposed act by a Minister of the Crown to be named by the Governor in Council; for the appointment of a registrar to receive, register and deal with applications for such investigations, and for the appointment of commissioners from time to time by the Governor in Council to hold investigations; for the payment of the registrar, commissioners and witnesses and to establish such offices, with assistants, as may be required; for power to remit or reduce duties where combines are proved to exist; for the revocation of patent rights in certain cases; for prosecution by the Attorney General of any province, or upon his failure to act, by the Solicitor General; and for the imposition of penalties for violation of the provisions of the proposed legislation.
Explain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will make the explanation at the moment that I thought of making on the introduction of the bill. It will cover the same ground.
Combines

There is at the present time no effective legislation against combines which are operating or may operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, whether producers, consumers or others. Such legislation as has been enacted by this parliament on the subject of combines in restraint of trade, the enhancement of prices and the like, is divisible broadly into three groups: first, the legislation with respect to conspiracies and combinations in restraint of trade which is embodied in the Criminal Code. It was originally enacted in a statute passed in 1889, which statute was to all intents and purposes declaratory of the common law. In 1892 this act was repealed by the Criminal Code, but the substance of its essential provision was reenacted in section 520 of the code of that year. The section of the code was amended in 1900 and again I think in 1906 when the Criminal Code was under consideration. It now stands as section 498 of the Criminal Code in virtually the same words as the original enactment of 1889.
The second group of provisions dealing with combines in restraint of trade, or operating to the detriment of the public, were those of the Combines Investigation Act of 1910 which provides for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers.
The third group is comprised in the legislation embodied in the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919.
The Combines and Fair Prices Act repealed the Combines Investigation Act of 1910. Such protection, therefore, as that act may have been presumed to have afforded to the public was removed by the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919. On the other hand, the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919 was itself dependent upon the Board of Commerce Act and the functioning of the Board of Commerce under that act. As hon. members of the House know, the Board of Commerce, under the Board of Commerce Act, never did function properly and has ceased to exist, so that such protection as might have been presumed to be afforded consumers or producers under the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act also no longer exists. While the Board of Commerce Act is not effective in any of its provisions so far as the protection of the public is concerned, Section 11 of the Combines and Fair Prices Act provides that no prosecution can be commenced under section 498 of the Criminal Code except under the written authority of the Board of Commerce. That section is still in the statute and as long as the statute remains, such protection as the

Criminal Code may be assumed to have afforded producers and consumers is also of no effect.
The legislation which the government proposes to introduce, repeals the Board of Commerce Act 1919 and the Combines and Fair Prices Act 1919, in that way freeing the statutes of two enactments which have become dead letters. On the other hand, this repeal will have the effect of reviving what there may be of virtue in section 498 of the Criminal Code which relates to conspiracies or combinations in restraint of trade.
Now, it is recognized that there are distinct limitations in the matter of the protection of the public under the provisions of the Criminal Code. The legislation which the government is introducing proceeds on the theory that the reason why section 498 of the Criminal Code is of so little effect is not that there are no combinations that are detrimental to the public or that such combinations are rare, but rather that the existence of these combinations, and their method of operation is difficult to discover; that what is needed is effective machinery of investigation which will disclose the existence of combines operating to the detriment of the public, and afford the information whereby proceedings under the Criminal Code can be made really effective in the case of individuals who are violating its provisions, or who are associated with combines that are operating to the detriment of the public. The legislation to be introduced provides machinery for investigation which it is hoped and believed will be effective toward this end. I will describe the proposed method of investigation a little more in detail when I refer to that particular phase of the subject.
The bill proposes to supplement the clause in the present Criminal Code by a provision creating a new criminal offence; making it an offence for any person to be a party or privy to or knowingly to assist in the formation or operation of a combine operating to the detriment of the public-a combine as defined in the legislation which is proposed. It will be readily observed that to be effective, the definition of the word " combine " must be made sufficiently comprehensive to include any agreement or arrangement, whether tacit, implied or expressed, which has the effect in practice of creating a combination that is operating against the public interest; and the definition of the word " combine ", as set forth in the proposed legislation, has been drafted with the end in view of having it sufficiently broad to include all possibilities under that head. On the other hand, that

Combines
parties may' be properly protected in the matter of criminal prosecutions and in order that no one may be prosecuted without having the advantages which the courts of law and the procedure in the courts throw about one who is brought before them for trial, a provision is included in the proposed legislation to the effect that no prosecution can take place except at the instance of the Attorney General of a province or the Solicitor General of the Dominion.
The remedies that are proposed are first of all, as indicated, the remedy of publicity. There are some offences as to which publicity is more effective as a remedy than penalty. The law is drafted so as to make possible the widest publicity with respect to any offence under its provisions.
Then there is the remedy of penalty, to which I have already referred, as a result of criminal prosecution. There are other remedies which may be exercised as the circumstances warrant-for example where it would appear that in the case of an article of commerce the parties concerned were profiting by virtue of the tariff as it is, power is given to the Governor in Council to reduce or to abolish duties with respect to that particular article. Similarly, where a patent is being used to limit manufacture, or in other ways limit conpetition, to the detriment of the public, power is given for the revocation of the patent.
In the proposed legislation the government has sought to be guided by such experience as the country has had in the workings of previous legislation; to retain what may have been of value in the Combines Investigation Act of 1910, and what may have been of value in the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919, but to meet, as far as may be possible, what has been found defective or in the nature of limitation in the successful working of both these enactments. The Combines Investigation Act of 1910 provided that where any six persons were of the opinion that a combine existed which was detrimental to the public they might appear before any judge of a high court and make out a prima facie case. If they succeeded, the judge was required to report accordingly to the registrar appointed under the act. The registrar thereupon called upon the parties who had made out the prima facie case, and upon the parties concerned in the combine, each to name a representative for a board, the two to agree upon a third representative, and the three thus ' named were constituted a board of investigation, which board was given all the powers
of a court of record. When the board had made its report the Governor in Council was then free to take such action as was thought best in accordance with other provisions of the statute, provisions similar to those respecting the reduction of customs duties, the revocation of patents, and criminal proceedings, to which I have already alluded.
It was found under the Combines Investigation Act that obliging individuals in the first instance to associate themselves together and make out a prima facie case before a judge discouraged in large measure any investigation. The parties seemed to be under the impression-although the law did not give ground for it-that they would necessarily have to bear the expense of the preliminary investigation, and might have to bear the expense of the investigation before the board that was subsequently appointed. For that reason, and possibly others as well, the Combines Investigation Act of 1910 was not used to the extent expected at the time that that measure was passed.
In the present proposed legisation the objection which I have just referred to has been removed by not obliging the parties to get together and prove a case before a judge in the first instance, but by permitting parties who believe a combine is operating in restraint of trade to make direct application to the registrar to be appointed under this act, and giving power to the registrar himself to make an investigation to satisfy his own mind as to whether such a combination does exist or not. The act gives the registrar very full powers. He may, if he so desires, proceed on his own initiative. The act further provides that the government may appoint one or more commissioners, where it is shown before the registrar, or for other reasons there are grounds for believing that the combine is operating to the detriment of the public. The government may appoint these commissioners with all the powers that commissioners have under the Enquiries Act, take evidence under oath, visit the premises, inspect books, compel the production of documents, if they like. Ample provision is made to secure the due exercise of these powers. Under the Board of Commerce Act there was created an extraordinary court, a court of record with powers of inquisition, accusation and judgment, all exercisable by the same body. I will not go into the reasons which seemed to render a court of that kind valueless for the purpose for which it was instituted. I will simply point out that it had functions which seldom are combined in any one body, that namely of beginning investigation, of laying information, of prosecuting,
Combines

of pronouncing judgment and seeing to the enforcement of that judgment. It moreover was a single court, constituted of a definite personnel; it was supposed to have and did have virtually the whole say as to what prosecutions should be commenced, even as I have already indicated, for violations of the Criminal Code. Experience has Bhown that a board of that kind cannot be expected to function properly, and instead, therefore, of a board of that character, this measure proposes to give full power of investigation to commissioners to be specially appointed from time to -time as occasion may require.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that that broadly is the outline of the proposed legislation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I do not think any great object could be served by a prolonged discussion, but I felt that I could say something anent the historical summary given by the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I remark first of all that the title of the bill, as it appears in the introduction of bills, and as it is summarized again, reflected at least in this motion, is not in accord with what was promised in the Speech from the Throne. The Speech from the Throne promised legislation "to safeguard the interests of producers and consumers" against Trust monopolies and combines, thereby foreshadowing, not investigatory legislation, but executory legislation, legislation that would itself have a controlling and final authority over such trusts, monopolies and combines. The promising language of the Speech from the Throne was considerably modulated when the title of the bill came down-"an Act to Provide for the Investigation of Combines, Monopolies, Trusts and Mergers." The Enquiries Act today would give us as ample powers of investigation as anyone would wish, that is to say, if the contemplated legislation is for investigation, and nothing further. The Combines Investigation Act was, it is true, repealed by the Combines and Pair Prices Act, 1919. The Combines Investigation Act provided for the investigation of trusts or mergers upon information of six persons and certain responsibilities taken by them not of a financial character. That act was on the statute books for a good many years. It was an investigatory act, that is to say, it looked to investigation and investigation alone. There could be no prosecution under it but there was one investigation commenced, in the course of its long existence. That was against the United Shoe Machinery Company. That company was charged with being a trust combine within the meaning of that act. The necessary com-[Mr. Mackenzie King, j
plaint was laid, and the whole paraphernalia of the act was gone through. It lasted some years, went through some of the courts, cost many thousands of dollars, and as the end approached, it appeared that by the time the end was reached we would be exactly where we began, assuming we would succeed. In a word, after all the machinery of the act was exhausted, one had to start all over again and prosecute the alleged combine monopoly or trust, adduce again the evidence before the court, call upon the court for injunction restraining proceedings, and in the meantime of course the company under investigation would simply have to alter its procedure by such degree or by such angle as evidently would comply with the dictum that may have been secured from the judge in the process of the investigation, which done, it would be quite absolved from liability under the effective prosecution that would follow. In a word, the presence of the act, in so far as it was a necessary preliminary to prosecution, was really a buffer as between the consumer and producer on the one hand and the trust and merger on the other. It would have been better and more effective legislation to have had the criminal code in effect alone, and have machinery provided whereby the company, the trust or combine, could be prosecuted under the terms of the code. The Combines and Fair Prices Act was passed in 1919, and that, in conjunction with its accompanying legislation, the Board of Commerce Act, provided a body and endowed it with power to do what the Prime Minister fairly describes, namely, lay-not institute-proceedings itself when it had reason to believe that trusts were operating in restraint of trade, a, combine against the interests of the public. Whatever may be said of those two acts -I do not for one moment say they were not subject to criticism, and that weaknesses did not develop-it cannot be said that ample powers were not given to the Board of Commerce, the board that was entrusted with the enforcing of both statutes. The powers given were wide and sweeping-wider than had ever been given before in any country in the world; in fact they were undoubtedly in my judgment too wide, and as a consequence of that-perhaps there were other causes as well *-when the proceedings brought wrere called in question and challenged before the courts, the courts held that parliament in endeavouring to arm the board with power to control the depredations of trusts and combines had gone beyond its jurisdiction. Since that time, while the statutes have remained, they are not effective statutes because there has been no board operating. The

Combines
Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) states that a section in one of these acts, I think the Combines and Fair Prices Act, provides that the interposition of the Board of Commerce and its authority shojild be secured before there should be criminal prosecution under section 498 of the code and that, inasmuch as these two acts still exist, although not operative, criminal presecutions are now forbidden. If that be the case, it had not been drawn to my attention. Undoubtedly that should be removed and there should be a re-establishment of the full right of prosecution under the code.
Another section provided for the repeal of the Combines Investigation Act of earlier years. This, of course, was necessary as a new, much more cofnplete and drastic method was being adopted.
The experience of these years has led me to one main conclusion. Before I mention it, I will make some reference to what I understand by the Prime Minister's explanation. So far as I can gather from his explanation, what he purposes to do is substantially to reinstate the old Combines Investigation Act, not in its exact terms, because there are some alterations. There are to be registrars or commissioners appointed before whom complaints are to be laid and who are to have investigatory powers. Apparently, they are to exercise some of the functions which under the old act, were exercised by the courts of the land. I have not much hope of that being an improvement. What I apprehend is this, that this bill, when it comes, will not get any further than the old act, and that means that it will simply compel prosecution to travel in a circle and to traverse the circle twice instead of once.
In the United States, they have approached the subject in another way. The Federal Trade Commission has certain powers; but the government of the country, having established laws which define trusts, monopolies, combines and restraints of trade, having limited the activities in scope and character, of trusts, monopolies and combines, then take it upon themselves to execute these laws and to institute prosecutions for violations of their law, such prosecutions requiring the readjustment of the whole merging companies. They operated this legislation against the United Shoe Machinery Company; but they had much better success than we could ever have had under the old act. The government of the United States, carrying on its prosecution, obtained the judgment of the Supreme Court of the United States, declaring that this company's methods of operation, were illegal, assessing them with damages for the same,
and demanding that within a certain time the whole method be altered. It has been altered, very much, undoubtedly, to the loss of the company; but at all events effective curtailment has taken place, because the principle of government responsibility for prosecution is embodied in the United States legislation. The initiative is there; the powers are there, effective powers and not merely circuitous, ambitory and purposeless powers. I hope this bill will go further than we are led to expect from the title; in a word that there will be something executory, final and effective about it, and it will not be merely a repetition of the old act, the Combines Investigation Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would ask my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) to judge the proposed legislation, not by the title, but by its provisions. As he well knows, a title is meaningless when it comes to courts of law and positive action, but the provisions of an enactment are everything. I think my right hon. friend will find, that all that was promised in the Speech from the Throne that:- A bill will be submitted to you- to safeguard the interests of consumers and producers from undue enhancement of prices or unfair restriction of trade by combines, monopolies, trusts, or mergers.
[DOT]-has been adequately met in the proposed legislation.
I may mention to my right hon. friend the reason which has prompted the government to lay particular emphasis oh the investigation aspect of the legislation. I pointed out, in speaking on the measure at the outset, that the difficulty of proceeding under the Criminal Code has been found to be due, not to the circumstances that combines are rare or that they do not occasion restraint of trade, but to the fact that their existence and particularly their method of operation, is sometimes very difficult to discover, and the only way in which it can be brought to light is by thorough and full powers of investigation. The section in the Criminal Code relating to conspiracies and combines in restraint of trade differs from most other sections of the code in this particular, that other offences under the code are, for the most part, obvious, whereas the existence and operation of combines is not. If murder, or theft, or perjury is committed, the fact is known at once, and the main difficulty of those whose duty it is to enforce the law is to apprehend the offender and bring him before the courts. But when the matter is one of the existence or operation of a combine, the difficulty is, not to apprehend the offender, once he is known, but to find out first of all to what extent he is operating
Combines

against the public interest; to make clear the nature and extent of the offence. That can be done only by giving very full powers of investigation, and for that reason the government has thought it well to lay particular emphasis on the investigation feature of the legislation.
As to the proposed legislation being something more than a mere act of investigation, I would like to quote just one clause which appears in the bill and which is in the nature of the creation of a new offence. I only hope that when we come to enacting this clause, my right hon. friend and those who sit around him will not raise the objection that it goes too far and that it is likely, perhaps, to effect more in the way of concrete, executive action than he and his friends would like. The clause reads:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding $10,000 or to two years' imprisonment, or if a corporation to a penalty not exceeding $25,000, who is a party or privy to or knowingly assists in the formation or operation of a combine as defined in this act.
The definition of "combine" as given in the act reads:
The expression "combine" in this act shall be deemed to have reference to such combines immediately hereinafter defined as in the opinion of the registrar or any commissioner have operated or are likely to operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others; and limited as aforesaid, the expression as used in this act shall be deemed to include (1) mergers, trusts and monopolies socalled, and (2) the relation resulting from the purchase, lease, or other acquisition by any person of any control over or interest in the whole or part of the business of any other person, and (3) any actual or tacit contract, agreement, arrangement or combination which has or is designed to have the effect of (i) limiting facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing; or, (ii) preventing, limiting or lessening manufacture or production; or (iii) fixing a common sale or a resale price, or a common rental, or a common cost of storage or transportation; or (iv) enhancing the price, rental or cost of article, rental storage or transportation; or (v) preventing or lessening competition in, or substantially controlling within any particular area or district or generally, production, manufacture, purchase, barter, sale, storage, transportation, insurance or supply; or (vi) otherwise restraining or injuring trade or commerce.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have not the two provisions side by side, but if my right hon. friend will make a comparison of them when we are in committee on the bill he will find that of the two definitions this is very much broader and goes very much further than the Criminal Code as it stands to-day. As my right hon. friend has pointed out, the word "unduly" does appear in the code where it does not appear in this definition; and he will also find elsewhere in the code the word "unreasonably". But there are other particulars in which this definition is broader, and I will indicate them to the House when I have the two provisions side by side so as to be able to compare them. With respect to what my right hon. friend has said as to this legislation re-enacting some of the provisions of the Combines and Investigation Act of 1910, let me say to him and to the House at once that it does. But I would draw his attention to this fact, that the legislation of 1919 also reenacted certain of the provisions of the act of 1910. For example, the Combines and Fair Prices Act and the Board of Commerce Act between them re-enacted the provision giving the Governor in Council power to reduce duties, which appeared for the first time in the Combines Act of 1910, and also re-enacted the provision with respect to the revocation of patents, and as well, I think, with respect to providing information for criminal prosecutions.
These are in the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919; they are the law to-day.

speechtext:
As I have said, the object of this legislation is to retain anything of value in the previous legislation. I am quite willing to go halves with my right hon. friend as to the previous legislation, both his and the legislation I had to do with, not meeting the case fully. I think it has all been by way of experiment with a very difficult subject; and I believe that the experience, both under the act of 1910 and

Supply-Public Works
under the legislation of 1919, will be helpful to this House in deciding upon the worth of the parts of the legislation which we have retained and of the new clauses which we have introduced. Our aim has been to take from all existing or past legislation what is likely to be effective and helpful and to add additional features where there has been something lacking in the law as it stands or previously stood; for our desire is to place on the statutes an act which will be of real service to consumers and producers alike in protecting them against the operations of combines which may be detrimental to the public interest.

Under this heading I want to ask the minister what he has done towards restoring to the city of Portage la Prairie the facilities for its sewerage outlet of which this government deprived it by the construction of a ditch in the Assiniboine river in 1908. I have been in communication with the minister on the matter, as also have the city and the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. Leader). The latest information I have is that no progress at all has been made and I see nothing in the estimates to indicate that there will be any progress. This estimate is the same as it was a year ago; but this sum stipulated here, if it were all applied to the one purpose, would not, ac-
4 p.m. cording to my information, be a beginning towards the repairing of the damages which the government caused that city. We are right now at the edge of spring; the minister knows the circumstances, I need not at this moment detail them, because he is fully aware of them. But already about eight months of delay have occurred and no matter what the government does now there are sure to be somewhat serious conditions. I am sorry indeed that no provision is made here, because this vote is not for Portage la Prairie work and in any event is quite insufficient for anything practical. The government cannot make speed enough to repair this damage, and apparently no effort is being made to do anything at all. I hope for a more favourable reply and a more definite statement than has yet been obtainable from the department.
On December 6, 1921, I was elected representative for the city of Portage la Prairie.
Whom did you defeat?

For the information of the House, and incidentally for the information of the right hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Meighen), I want to say that up to this time I have not delegated my duties to anyone else, nor do I intend to do so. I leave that to a higher tribunal.
Now, let me say a word in regard to this item. Last year a serious condition prevailed in Manitoba through the overflowing of the Assiniboine river. I brought the matter to the attention of the government, and instead of throwing brickbats at the administration, as we sometimes have to do, I want to throw a bouquet to-day; I want to thank them for coming to the assistance of the settlers along the Assiniboine river and to voice the appreciation of my constituents in Portage la Prairie for the prompt action taken in that connection. I pointed out last year that this question of repairing the dykes along the Assiniboine river had been a live one for the last forty years. The banks of that river overflow periodically, and usually no attention is paid to the matter until on the eve of an election, when some candidate is promised that assistance will be given. In that respect I cannot exonerate either of the late governments; both were guilty. I suggest to the government to-day that they take this matter up and, in conjunction with the province or perhaps with the municipalities, enter into some kind of arrangement under which such a situation may be taken care of in the future. As it is now, nobody seems to be willing to take the responsibility. There is no doubt in my mind that the Dominion government is liable, because the river, having been declared a navigable stream, is certainly under the jurisdiction of the federal authority, and the province has very properly declined to assume the responsibility. But I believe that an arrangement could be made whereby the situation would be taken care of without reference to election promises-that is Progressive politics. I have been negotiating with the government for some time with respect to the diversion of the waters of the Assiniboine river from their original channel and the resulting exposure of the mouth of the sewer outlet from the city of Portage la

Prairie, but I must admit that the government have been very slow in the matter. I know, however, that they have had their engineers over the ground; various estimates have been made and various solutions of the problem advanced. I would like to know from the government-in fact, I may tell the House that I do know, but for the information of the hon. members I would ask the minister to tell us what proposal he has in mind to take care of the situation that has developed at Portage la Prairie.

speechtext:
The right hon. leader of the
Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) are right in assuming that there is no appropriation under this item for taking care of the sewers at Portage la Prairie. The right hon. gentleman stated in his opening remarks that this government had failed. That is not right; the government are dealing with conditions as they found them. The government of Canada probably did fail. This work was designed and carried through at the request of the people of Portage la Prairie and adjoining districts. In 1908, on account of the lands being flooded, they asked the Dominion government to construct a channel that would carry off the overflow during the high water period. If the work had been carried out as designed by the engineers, probably the difliculties we find today would not exist. However, appropriations were not forthcoming and the work was neglected, with the result that the main stream became diverted and to-day the bed of the river is in the new channel, leaving the sewer pipe from the town of Portage in the old channel and causing it to discharge at this season of the year on an empty river bed. That is undoubtedly a serious matter from the point of view of the public health of the citizens of Portage. When it was brought to my attention last year I took a sympathetic attitude ana 'nstituted a careful investigation to see in what way the Department of Public Works could afford relief in connection with a difficulty that had developed, to some extent, through its own activities. But we found a rather peculiar disposition on the part of those controlling the affairs of the people of Portage la Prairie. Evidently they are going to sit back and continue to cry for help from the Dominion government. I am desirous of assisting them, but I would like to see them trv to do something for themselves. Undoubtedly the work was originally carried out for the advantage of the people of the town and the adjoining territory; in fact, it was constructed

on their application. We are trying to negotiate with the council with a view to arriving at an agreement in the matter. I have had a report made by the district engineer, supported by a report submitted by the late Chief Engineer, Mr. St. Laurent. I have a recommendation that I propose to make to council if we can succeed in our negotiations with the citizens of Portage la Prairie. I am of the opinion that the Dominion government should supply the funds necessary to extend the sewer pipe from its present position into the new bed of the river or into another portion of the river, and that, I think, is as far as the Department of Public Works should go. Apparently, however, that is not the wish of the citizens of Portage la Prairie; at least, they have not so stated to us. The matter is under negotiation.	I
think that is a fairly clear statement of the facts.
What does the government propose to do about the Assiniboine a little higher up, at the town of Brandon-

Perhaps the hon. member will permit me to interrupt; we are not through with this phase of it yet. I did not know I had represented myself, Mr. Chairman, as the member for Portage la Prairie. I quite recognize that the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Leader) was elected for that constituency at the last election. Notwithstanding that fact, however, it so turns out that I have been requested to take this matter up by the council of the city of Portage la Prairie. Having such authority I do not require the further authority of the hon. member. I have been written to repeatedly and asked to assist the city 'in the matter, by the clerk as well as by the mayor. What I want is to get this work done and get the minister's promise to do it now. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie can have the glory-if he so desires. I had in no way reflected on him.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question?
Oh, yes.

The hon. gentleman is very kind. He said he had been requested by the mayor and council and by different citizens of Portage to take the matter up. Does he not think it was an ungracious act to bring it up here in the parliament of Canada without consulting the proper representative of Portage la Prairie?

I am looking after the city as I was asked to do-I am not looking

Supply-Public Works
after the representative. I was about to remark that when an hon. member of this House spurns assistance in any effort for his constituents, it does not speak very highly of his judgment.

I did not spurn the efforts;
I objected to his manner of presenting them.

I am presenting the matter to the government, not to the hon. member. I wish to give some history of this matter, and I think it will show to the committee that I am not at fault in being somewhat concerned. I know of the subject from its commencement, I say in answer to the minister's assertion that there should be an effort on the part of the city to help themselves out of this difficulty that the difficulty in which the city finds itself is due originally to the action of the government of Canada, and it is now due to the inaction of this government-to its delay in meeting the situation. The cause of the trouble was the work of a former government, the government of 1908. When I give an account of this construction as it developed in the fall of that year, hon. members will understand that the responsibility is not on the city but on this government, and that this government has no reasonable excuse for not coming to parliament now and in this vote and asking for an appropriation to remedy a state of affairs created by the government of 1908. The responsibility for finding a solution and putting the city in the position it was in up to 1922 is on this administration and it is on no one else. It is not on the city at all.
The city of Portage la Prairie is situated to the north of the Assiniboine river. The Assiniboine river immediately to the south takes a bend in the shape of a horse shoe, the ball of the horse shoe being projected northward almost up to the city. In the year* 1902 and 1904, years of great flood in that locality, the river overflowed its banks, not at Portage la Prairie, but to the east of Portage la Prairie, and flooded farm lands in very large area between that city and the city of Winnipeg causing very considerable damage. The government of the country was appealed to, to remedy that situation. The method of doing so was not directed at all in the petitions to this government. The method was left to the government. The government chose to seek a remedy by digging a ditch across the horse shoe between the one extremity and the other, thereby diverting to the extent the ditch would divert the course of the river from going around the horse shoe. Such was the method the government adopted. It
was pointed out indeed it was feared at the time that if this were done there would be a probability of the horse shoe drying up. Now at the time this was done in 1908, at that very time and for three years before the city had had constructed a sewerage system which emptied into the horse shoe, which emptied into the part from which the water was about to be diverted. All went well, of course, until the ditch widened in extent, and that happened gradually through these years, but chiefly of late years, and last year it had proceeded to such an extent that the ditch the government dug in 1908 became the course of the river, and the whole horse shoe was deserted by the water altogether and dried up. The consequence is that the sewerage of the whole city is emitted on dry land at the very verge of the city right in the neighbourhood of a fairly well populated farming district. Such is the consequence of the government's action.
Now the minister wants to imply that in some way the city of Portage la Prairie was a party to the action of the government in 1908'. Not at all. But before I come to that let me give just another phase of this story. This was a piece of work done on the favourite plan of the present government, the foreman and day labour plan. The floods were in 1902 and 1904. The petition was on January 10, 1905. The communications to the then government, the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, of which I see more than one member sitting in front of me now as a member of this government were in 1905. The communications came in January, 1905, the only petition that ever came was presented in that month. On that petition there is not the name of one man who was a citizen of Portage la Prairie at that time. All were farmers or residents between that city and the city of Winnipeg. Not only did the city not petition or become a party thereto in any way, but no resident of the city was a petitioner. The government did it without any acquiescence of any sort and without consulting in any way the city of Portage la Prairie.
Did the government do anything in answer to the petition? Not in 1905, not in 1906, not in 1907. In these years there was no general election on or pending. The government waited until the general election of 1908. The election was on the 26th of October, 1908, and the 19th of September of that year the Laurier government placed down there a number of men, a very large number for the work, and put them in charge of a good Liberal foreman, kept them all well corralled in the ditchj and marched them up in caravans on election day in order to make sure of defeating me in that contest. Of course, when the elec-
Supply-Public Works

tion was over, the government's sense of responsibility ceased because the government's object ended, and the men were all taken out on the 31st of October, five days after the election was decided.
Mr, KING (Kootenay): The government's responsibility did not cease then in regard to this ditch, although that government has disappeared.

That is what I am trying to impress upon the minister. I seem to have succeeded more rapidly than I expected. It did not cease, it still exists. On the 31st of October, the election being safely by, though they were frustrated in Portage la Prairie, they took all the men out, did not complete the work that was projected then, just left it as it was. What was apparently projected, though at that time I did not know it, was that there should be something in the- nature of a weir placed at the entrance of the ditch so as to provide that a share of the water would still flow around the curve. This was not done. As a consequence, the ditch that formerly was 20 feet wide at the bottom now is nearly 200 feet wide, and very deep; The whole river is diverted, and the city of Portage la Prairie is entirely without an outlet for its sewerage. Who then can suggest for a minute that the responsibility for such a state of affairs is not on the government, and the whole responsibility? The responsibility for finding a remedy is on the government. It is not on us.
I put a question on this subject in parliament on the 3rd of February, 1909, and I obtained an answer which I have now before me showing that the petitions all came in in January, 1905; that nothing was done until September, 1908; that everything was done between the 19th day of September and the 31st day of October of that year, the election being safely passed; that it was not done by tender and contract, and that no provision whatever was made for taking care of the sewerage outlet of the city. Here is the weighty reason given by the government for not doing so. I asked:	[DOT]
What, if any, provision has been made by the government for disposal of the sewerage of the city of Portage la Prairie, as the present method of disposal of same is said to be interfered with by the work so done?
Here is the answer:
No provision has been made as this is a public work, constructed by the government, at the request of citizens of Portage la Prairie, and for the benefit of the city and the adjoining country.
It was not for the benefit of the city at all; it was not at the request of the citizens, nor of any of the citizens. It was done for the I Mr. Meighen.]
benefit of others farther down, or supposed to be for their benefit. I presume it did work for their benefit, although a better method could have been found. The city of Portage la Prairie was a stranger to it altogether. Why all these months of hesitation? It was a political ditch dug for a political purpose, to defeat an opponent of the government at that time. That is why the work was done at the time it was done and in the way it was done. The damage caused the city is now seen. Work that originally cost some five thousand odd dollars has caused the city damage which to repair along the line now suggested by the minister, but for which he does not provide,-by extending the sewer on to meet the ditch-will cost according to the minister's engineer, $65,000.

Will the hon. gentleman
state what he did as private member for Portage la Prairie, as Solicitor General, as Minister of the Interior, and finally as Prime Minister to remedy the situation?

The situation did not need remedying when I was there. The water was flowing around the bend. But if the present condition had developed it would have been remedied and eight months would not have been lost with the sewerage emptying into the dry bed of the stream.
But two years were lost.

We were often called upon when in office to remedy the blunders of hon. members opposite, but we waited until the evil appeared before applying the cure. If we had set out to take care of this case before the damage arrived then we would have been told we were wasting money and that no damage would ever develop.
Mr, CANNON: If the evil did not exist how could my right hon. friend mention this matter in 1909?

I asked some questions in 1909. I had a fear it would come and I said so. There is no need of meeting damage until it is at least in sight, but a government that puts off dealing with an evil when it does appear is responsible for the consequences. If we had been in power when the time for action arrived, we would have been obliged to remedy the consequences of the folly of hon. members opposite.

My hon. friend no doubt is taking a great interest in this question and has made a reference back as far as 1909. But he is probably also aware

Supply-Public Works
that in 1917 and 1918 the engineers did deal with this work. They made certain recommendations, and my right hon. friend failed to get a vote to carry out those recommendations. Had the recommendations been carried out this condition would not have existed.

Day by day and in eyery way I am learning more about politics. The information which the right hon. the leader of the Opposition has conveyed to the committee to-day was dug up as a result of a lot of hard work and at my own private expense and submitted to the city council of Portage la Prairie. What my right hon. friend has said in regard to the digging of this canal in 1908 is true. I am not a politician. I do not owe allegiance to either one of the old parties and I never shall.

You are too young
yet.

I want to be fair in anything that I say. When the right hon. gentleman was a minister in the federal government and the Hon. Robert Rogers was Minister of Public Works in the same administration, the Provincial Treasurer of Manitoba, Hon. Hugh Armstrong wrote Mr. Rogers a letter on the eve of the provincial election, telling him that if he would grant some money to do work along the Assiniboine river in the constituency of Lakeside no doubt it would prove very popular. The right hon. gentleman, (Mr. Meighen), as hon. members know, was member for Portage la Prairie for a great many years but ceased to occupy that position in 1921. This situation has been developing since 1913, and I saw a letter sent from his law partner at the last Dominion election, subsequent to dissolution, asking the city of Portage la Prairie to take this matter up. Consequently I assume that the right hon. gentleman was fully conversant with the situation while he was member for Portage la Prairie. During that time why did he not do something to relieve the situation? Why he is doing so much worrying now I cannot understand. I realize that I have not had much experience in politics, but so long as I am member for Portage la Prairie I am going to represent that constituency to the very best of my ability; and when I want anybody to help me I will ask for that assistance. I asked the right hon. gentleman to help me when T came down to Ottawa last year and he said "Harry, I will do anything I can for you." Yet
Supply-Public Works

he makes a long statement to the committee this afternoon on this matter without saying a word to me on the subject. My right hon. friend says that I am thin-skinned. Let me inform him that he has been discourteous to me, and I resent it.

It is not my intention to speak at any great length, but I must say that I am pleased to discover that Portage la Prairie is so happily situated as to possess two members. In that respect Portage la Prairie is one of the most favoured constituencies in the Dominion. I was considerably surprised to find only the paltry sum of $41,265 in the estimates of the Public Works de1-partment for Manitoba. Of course we have no harbours in my riding although- we have lots of home brew. However, what I want to mention is this: The Assiniboine was in flood last year and if it had risen about six inches more a lot of water from Portage la Prairie would have been thrown into Pro-veneher. We would not like that, because the electors of Provencher do not want the waters of Portage la Prairie running over their ground; those waters are very troublesome waters. I think the Minister of Public Works should really give this matter prompt and earnest attention because it is very serious in its nature not only to the electors of Portage la Prairie but also to a certain number of electors in the county which I represent. If the Minister of Public Works does not take this matter into very serious consideration there will probably be some very hot arguments, and perhaps even fighting, between Provencher and Portage la Prairie.
What I am most anxious about is to get some statement from the minister as to what he is actually going to do and when.
I do not wish to prolong this discussion, it is not really in order.
Yes, it is.
However, let us get done with it.
Certainly, the discussion is in order.
I think not, not on the present item.
When would it be in order?

Do not let us misunderstand the situation. This is not a new matter. We find that the district engineer in

1917, and again in 1918, recommended widening the cut, but not deepening if, as he feared the cut might become the main channel of the river and leave the city sewer outlet dry. It was proposed as part of the work to build a weir, or barrier, at the mouth or upstream end of the cut to prevent further scouring from deepening the cut, but funds were not made available for this purpose. Had it been constructed, its efficiency for the purpose intended would be doubtful in the soil at that point. Between 1918 and the flood of 1922 the yearly floods had -widened the cut to about 50 feet and deepened it to 12 feet below top of bank.
Now if it is a question of fixing the responsibility it is not difficult to do that in the light of the report which I have referred to. If the work had been carried on as recommended by the engineer in 1919 there would not have been the condition we find to-day. It is true that a great flood occurred in the spring of 1922. As far as we are concerned, this matter has engaged the attention of the department, and we are prepared to deal fairly with the city of Portage. I have made a proposal to them. We have an estimate of the cost of replacing this sewer in connection with the new channel and the figure has been placed at $45,000. I will recommend to the government of Canada, and I hope to this House, that a sum be given for that purpose. We will give the money to the city and let them restore the sewer. But it is not the intention of the Department of Public Works to construct the sewer system for the city of Portage la Prairie.
The minister proposes to offer the city $45,000 to continue the sewer on down. I presume that is the estimate of the department as to what it will cost.
Yes.
I saw it stated as $65,000. Suppose the department, which will exercise some supervision over it, finds that it costs more, will the department provide the money?

I am advised that this will be about the cost. The department has received a report on the matter. I may say the department does not want to injure the city. We want to help them, and this is an estimate which has been made. The thing will be checked carefully and a proper estimate made for the work.

The intention of the government is to provide for the extension down, such extension to be constructed of course at reasonable cost.

Supply-Public Works
Yes.
I understand the minister gives an affirmative answer.
Yes.

I am very glad, and now I onlj' add, no petition came from Portage la Prairie to me to have this work done while I was in office. There may have been individual communications, but I cannot recall one. The matter never came to a head till 1922, as the hon. minister said, and there was no reason to take action sooner. It was time enough in 1922 to deal with the matter. All I am complaining about is the delay since August, 1922, because the communication reached the minister, if not in July, early in August, setting forth fully the situation.

I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a further matter in connection with the Assiniboine river. On the westerly part of the city of Winnipeg that river is eating away part of my constituency. As any one who knows these western rivers will realize, the rivers are apt to encroach. This river continually curves and is apt to encroach on the land with very serious damage in the case of urban municipalities. Inhere has been considerable communication from the municipality of St. James with regard to the waters in that district encroaching on the land. It seems to me that some provision should be made to take care of this situation. I should like to call attention to, the situation as it prevails higher up the river, at the city of Brandon. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) is not here, but we have talked over this matter, and I think I am not encroaching on his territory when I speak of this. There was a . very serious flood in Brandon last spring. In the district generally known locally as the flats " hundreds of homes were flooded. Immense damage was caused, not only to the houses but to the gardens in the vicinity. Many of the poorer people of that district lost their all. I understand that the department gave assurances that, although damages could not be given- and I do not see why damages could not be given for this-that at least an investigation would be held and the department would see to it if possible that a similar flood would not recur. It is a very serious thing when it is considered that several thousand people live in the north end of Brandon and that in springtime when the water is high they may have their homes flooded. Is anything definite being done to prevent a recurrence of this flooding?

The government does not hold itself responsible for the natural erosion caused by floods in Canadian rivers. That would be a tremendous undertaking. It is being grappled with throughout Canada. I know that in our far western provinces the municipalities and the provincial governments do a good deal towards the protection of the banks. At times the Dominion government have assisted where it seems the public interests have demanded it. But it has never been intended or acknowledged that the government would undertake to prevent erosions of these banks from floods or other natural causes, or to give protection to a community where lands have been flooded at times.
Mr. HOEY [DOT]' In the absence of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) I would like to ask the minister if a survey was promised in connection with the district immediately surrounding Brandon city, and if so has that survey been undertaken? I was given to understand that this survey had been promised with the object of readjusting conditions, so that floods in the future would be rendered almost impossible.

I think there was a suggestion last year and we did instruct the district engineer to keep in touch with the flood conditions and I am advised that he made a report during the summer on that question.
Is there any provision in this particular vote for improvement on lake Killarney as recommended by the engineer of the department?
I think not.

I would like to call attention to conditions on a part of lake Manitoba. That lake has been steadily rising for the last three years, to the great damage of the settlers. in that vicinity. Very much of the land has been flooded in that district. I think some 5,000 acres in one municipality have been submerged in the last two years. It seems this condition arises periodically. It was flooded I think in 1902. About that time there was a period of high water for a few years and a great part of the country was flooded. For the last three years it has been rising again. I am informed that if the water rises another foot fifty per cent of the people west of Dog lake will have to leave their farms, and many have had to leave them already. Mixed farming is carried on very largely in that district and the farmers depend very largely on the wild hay to feed

Supply-Public Works

their cattle. This hay land has been flooded for the last two or three years, and they have to import the hay to feed the cattle. At the present price of cattle, a farmer cannot afford to pay the freight on hay for a long distance, let alone buy it, and I hope the government is doing something in this, connection. I think it was stated last year that they were taking measurements and trying to do something in this connection. Is this work being carried on?
I think there have been some investigations carried on, but as to committing the government to an expenditure of public money, that has not as yet been broached.

With regard to the improvements at Killarney, the minister s deputy the other day informed me that this improvement had been provided for in this vote. Apparently it has not. Will the minister reconsider his estimate and include that small amount? It is very necessary that it should be attended to.

I am not sure, but it is quite possible that it might be taken out of this vote of S15.000; I have not the information in regard to- it with me.
Red river-repairs to channel protection work, $4,000.
Is this for the protected channel at the mouth of the river. Is the work to be done by contract, or by this popular day labour system, or by the Department of Public Works at Selkirk?

The work consists of placing riprap alongside and inside the protection work, so as to strengthen it and to prevent damage by storms. In all probability this will be don<* under the direction of the engineering staff.

Item agreed to.
Selkirk wharf repairs, $13,665.
Are transfer works provided for in this figure for the repair slip at Selkirk?
I think not. The work consists of renewing the decking, replacing piles and deck structure where necessary, and placing stone filling and gravel on the approach.

Is it the purpose of the government to provide in this amount for transfer tracks? This winter there are eight steamboats on the repair slip at Selkirk. There is not room for them and they have to be carried out on the side. No transfer
IMr. llancroft.]
tracks are provided for this purpose. I understand provision of transfer tracks would not entail a very large expenditure, and at the present time the Department of Public Works had to supply blocking for keeping the ships in position. If transfer tracks were provided, there would be no necessity for supplying blocking for this purpose. I understand the government gets a fee for bringing those ships up, and this would, in a measure, cover the expenditure.
It would seem that transfer tracks are a necessity to the work there, and I am advised that a recommendation has been made to that effect.
Was the recommendation that something would be done?
I did not intimate that. There has been a recommendation from the engineering staff for that work; that it is necessary work. Provision is not made in this estimate.

Item agreed to.
St. Andrews dam, repairs to fishway, $1,100.
Will this work on the St. Andrews dam and also the work at Selkirk be done by the Public Works department at Selkirk?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Wanipigow, (Hole river) reconstruction of dam, $3,600.

This is for the reconstruction of a dam that was formerly built at the mouth of this river as it enters lake Winnipeg. I visited that district last summer, and I should like to remind the minister that building this dam will, in my humble judgment, be of comparatively little use unless the river itself is cleared of logs. I traversed that river some eight miles east of lake Winnipeg, and I experienced the utmost difficulty in doing so. I learned from the residents up there-there are not many of them-that the river was cleared some years ago; but it has become badly congested, particularly at certain points, and it seems to me that, in the interest of economy, this work of clearing the river of logs should be undertaken at the same time that this dam is being rebuilt. It is scarcely necessary to remind the minister that there is at present considerable traffic in this river owing to the operations of the Selkirk Mining Company. I should like to get a promise from the minister that this matter will be taken into consideration.
