Mi-. KING (Kootenay): Is my hon. friend speaking of drift wood resulting from lumbering operations?
The natural fall of the trees across the river.
I did not have it brought to my attention that it was necessary to clear the river. I will have inquiries made.

Item agreed to.
Saskatchewan and Alberta-harbours and rivers generally, repairs and improvements, $20,000.

This does not seem to be a very large item for two provinces such as Saskatchewan and Alberta, and when we compare it with the items we were discussing yesterday, I think we should receive credit when we take up some other items in connection with those provinces. I see that $20,000 was voted last year. How was it expended?

The expenditures apparently were very' light last year. At Fort McMurray, East Edmonton, there was an expenditure of $435, a small expenditure at Banff and another at Craven. The total expenditure was only $459.
Out of the $20,000 voted last year?
Yes.
I suppose this is put in just for padding, to make it appear that something is being done in these provinces.
I would not say that. This has been the custom for many years.
What is the nature of the work done as a result of the expenditure of $450?
Launching three floating wharves and putting them up on the river bank in the fall. The largest expenditure was made at Fort McMurray.
What works are in contemplation for the present year?
I am informed nothing is noted for expenditure under this appropriation at the present time.
What is done with the $19,600 that is not spent?
Not being expended, it would lapse.

What does the minister do with it? Is it left in the
public treasury or is it spent for some other purpose?
It lapses entirely.
Voting of this amount of money, *if there is no expenditure expected, seems to be an absurdity.

It will be readily seen that Saskatchewan is at a great disadvantage in not having room to place its wharves. The amount expended there is very small. The minister is probably aware that my attitude towards this "free gift" is that I do not favour it. Quite seriously. I am going to ask the minister for his reply to a question that has been passing through my mind. Let us suppose that two types of men whom I will describe, were to ask him a certain question. First, I will describe the two types of men. One of them has been producing grain at a loss for the last two years, and I need not more than state that such is the case, because many members know that is a fact. This man does not lack in either industry or efficiency, and through no fault of his own he is producing grain at a cost of perhaps $1.25 a bushel and selling it at 90 cents. That is one type. Another is the stock raiser who is producing stock that he cannot sell for more than about half of what it actually cost. I know that this is true because I have purchased such stock. Indeed, I should be ashamed to state the prices at which I purchased some last fall, were it not for the fact that I bought it at an auction sale which was open to everybody. What would one expect these men to say to the minister? Why, they would say: We are carrying on our business at a heavy loss, drawing from our capital, and getting no assistance; and why should we carry our own burden and the other fellow's as well? Why should these people pay in taxes, as they do, their share of the hundreds of thousands of dollars that are levied-yes, and more than that, one might say millions-
We are all paying for your railways.

I see that the truth strikes home. You can always tell when it cuts, because you hear a howl. As I was saying, however, why should these people carry their own burden and be called upon to shoulder the burden of other people by enabling the government, not to carry out great undertakings for the good of the whole country, but to do little things to help industries which are in no greater distress than their own? I do not want to be offensive, but I
Supply-Public Works

ask a plain question to which I should like a plain answer: Why should these men carry , their own burden and the burden of those who are not as badly off as themselves?
I should desire to be sympathetic with both parties.

Item agreed to.
British Columbia-harbours and rivers generally, $75,000.
Is any provision being made for the renewal of the work on the contract relating to the dry dock in North Vancouver?

Not under this
item.
Is there any other item under which this matter might be discussed?

My hon. friend will have an opportunity to deal with this matter under the item relating to govem-men dry dock expenditures at Victoria, which will come up later. I shall be glad to have the subject discussed then.

That is in regard to Victoria. But this is the item under which are discussed all matters connected with docks and waters in the province. This is where the general discussions take place. The discussion might be admitted under the item with regard to the Victoria dock, but there would be far more reason for ruling it out under that item than under this one. In fact, there could be no reason for ruling it out here. It is under the vote for harbours and rivers generally that all matters of this kind come up for discussion.
I am not objecting to the hon. member discussing the matter he has raised. He asked me whether there was any other item under which he might bring it up and I simply informed him that there was.
I am not objecting to the 'answer that the minister has given the hon. member. I am merely pointing out that it would be more in order to discuss the matter now.	,

I was evidently misunderstood. I suggested that it might be an opportune time to take up the question when we were dealing with dry dock expenditures. But I have no objection to the discussion taking place now.

It would probably be advisable to refer briefly to the history of this matter. In 1910 an act was passed to en-
[Mr. Millar.j
courage the construction of dry docks throughout the Dominion of Canada. That act provided that the chief engineer of the department should certify as to the necessity for dry docks in various parts of the country, and the chief engineer has on various occasions certified to, and three governments have recognized, such a necessity in Vancouver. In February, 1920, authority was given for a subsidy under the act for the construction of a second-class graving dock. The parties to the contract were the Dominion government and the Coughlan Shipbuilding Company, and the subsidy was based on a valuation of $2,500,000, at 4i per cent, for a period of thirty-five years. A contract to that end was executed on October 27, 1920. In 1921, the Coughlan Company apparently found that it was not practicable to erect this second-class graving dock. It was an odd sort of dock anyway, and apparently they could not finance it. The result was that another shipbuilding company in Vancouver, the Wallace Company, negotiated with Coughlan's, and an arrangement was arrived at between them whereby the two interests should 5 p.m. combine and erect a floating dock. These two interests then came back to the government with revised plans for the floating dry dock. I may observe at this juncture that it was early in the summer of 1921, before any election was contemplated, that the negotiations were completed. And it was arranged with the government of that day that in consideration of the surrender of the old contract a new contract should be executed confirming the revised plan and giving the same subsidy. That contract was executed shortly before the election of 1921, and I have the personal assurance of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) that it is above suspicion. Since the execution of that ! contract the company has expended a very large sum of money; its commitments already amount roughly to 1400,000. Just after the election a telegram was sent by the department placing on the contract an embargo which has not been removed. Protests have been made by every conceivable organization in British Columbia interested in the matter, including the Vancouver Board of Trade, and boards of trade representing practically the whole of the lower mainland of British Columbia. The Shipping Federation of Canada has unanimously adopted a resolution urging upon the government the necessity of this project. Even the government's chief organ in British Columbia, the Vancouver World, has expressed in no

Supply-Public Works
uncertain terms its opinion that this work is necessary. I quote from an editorial in that paper1
In view of these facts, repudiation is impossible and unthinkable. Every consideration of national policy, of national honour and of national necessity-as well as every commercial necessity of the port of Vancouver requires the carrying out of the contract and the keeping of public faith. On the issue of public honour, there is no room for evasion, repudiation or compromise. On the fact of commercial necessity there is no room for argument-the need of docking and repair facility is a recognized need of every active port. There is no answer to the justice of this claim and right.
In answer to these protests the Prime Minister stated that the Minister of Public Works would, - at the close of the session of last year, proceed to Vancouver and investigate the matter further; he had already made some inquiry into it. The time for investigation has now passed, but we have no statement as to what is to be done. The contract still stands; the commitments made by reputable firms are such that the shipbuilding industry on the coast may be ruined. It is a recognized fact that there will be no shipbuilding for at least a period of years, and the only possibility of carrying on the industry is in securing the repair of the ships entering the harbour, the numbers of which are rapidly increasing. Cases where great loss has actually been sustained have been brought to the minister's attention. For instance, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have intimated that they are quite prepared to have _ repairs made in Vancouver that would run into at least $120,000 a year. Balfour, Guthrie and Company stated that in less than four years they would have spent almost $200,000 in dry dock work at Vancouver had there been facilities for doing so. The same applies to many other lines. A few years ago there were only two steamship lines entering Vancouver; to-day there are seventeen. The number of ships entering that port is increasing daily; it now largely exceeds the number entering the port of Montreal. Facilities have been provided for dry docking at practically every port in Canada. St. John has a dry dock; Halifax has one; Quebec, two; Montreal, two; Kingston, Collingwood, Toronto, Fort William, Prince Rupert and Victoria, all have their facilities, but the port which does the greatest volume of shipping has no facilities. If Vancouver is to continue as a great terminal shipping port, something will have to be done in this connection. Shipping companies will locate only in those ports where proper terminal facilities are available, and one of the prime requisites is dry dock facilities. Seattle has several dry docks, and for that reason 
many shipping companies will go there instead of to Vancouver. The delay in providing proper dry dock facilities at Vancouver will result in great loss of revenue to the country through loss of volume of business. The expense of the project would not be great, because the capital expenditure would be provided by private interests. The first year's outlay could not exceed $40,000, and for a period of thirty-five years the expenditure would be about $112,000 per annum. The Dry Dock Subsidies Act was passed for the express purpose of encouraging the construction of dry docks in our various ports, and to my mind it is unreasonable to refuse to grant a subsidy to the port which has a larger volume of shipping than that which can be claimed by any other port in the Dominion.

I am very glad my hon. friend has again brought this matter to the attention of the House. Dry dock construction on the Pacific coast seems to have had a rather stormy career; agitations have taken place over a period of very many years. What seemed rather to disturb the government on taking office was to find that a time when governments and people were trying to practise economy, we had two large works launched on the Pacific coast for dry dock purposes. There was a large commitment in respect to the dock at Victoria, which is now under construction and presumably is to be operated under government control; and there were also commitments under the Dry Dock Subsidies Act. It was found that no large expenditure had been made in connection with the work at Vancouver. It is true, the companies had arranged their organization, and purchased some plant and material, but the outlay was not very large.
I understand that figures have been furnished to the minister indicating an outlay on the part of the companies concerned of $398,000.

Expenditures, as I say, have been made, but not in proportion to the expenditures made by the government at Victoria. It was considered wise to hold this work in abeyance. The matter is receiving the attention of the government and I am in hopes that we may be able to advise the House of some conclusions in regard to it.

I wish to Bay a word
in reference to the Fraser river improvements. The minister is to be commended upon the interest which he has displayed in this important work. I appreciate the fact that it is receiving his attention. I also think that
Supply-Public Works

it is pretty generally agreed that he and his department are doing their best to provide a proper, safe and reliable channel from New Westminster to the gulf. We are not asking for a harbour to compete in any way with the harbour at Vancouver, which is only a matter of some fifteen or twenty miles from us by water and less than that by land. We appreciate the fact that Vancouver harbour is suitable for large shipping and we believe in the necessity for the improvements at Vancouver harbour. But on the Fraser river we have a somewhat different proposition. What we require there is a channel which will enable us to bring in ships more particularly for the purpose of taking care of the lumber which is manufactured on the Fraser river. It may not be generally known, but I think I n,m correct in saying that approximately one-third of the lumber and shingles manufactured in British Columbia and that is a very considerable amount, of course-is manufactured on the Fraser river; I am referring now to the main channel and also to the north arm. We have mills there which are doing an export business and shipping lumber to the markets of the world. A very large trade ha$ grown up, and a much bigger trade is in prospect providing it is possible for us to ship our lumber at reasonable rates. The rate by water compares very favourably with the rate by rail. For purposes of comparison I might mention that the rate from New Westminster by water to the eastern states, say to the port of New York, is no greater than the rate by rail from New Westminster to Calgary. That means that we have a very big market for some of our manufactured products, more particularly our shingles for which there is a very great demand in the eastern states. There is also a great demand, of course, for our other manufactured products. Our lumber is shipped to various parts of the world, and the demand for it is constantly growing.
Now, in order to economically ship our products we have to be able to bring vessels right into our docks. There is no reason why we should not do that providing the channel is put in proper shape, because with the exception of one or two shallow spots, the channel is sufficiently deep to take care of any lumber-carrying ships which might be expected to come in there. In that connection I might point out that the draught of lumber-carrying vessels is increasing. They are using much larger ships now than they did a few years ago. At one time the department under the previous government appointed a board of engineers to inquire into conditions on the Fraser river, and that board reported as to the class of vessels which might be ex-

pected to take lumber from our ports. In that report it was stated that the great majority of the ships which might be expected to do business with us were of comparatively light draught. I believe that that condition has changed and that larger ships are now in the business. It is necessary for us to have a depth of at least thirty feet. I believe that a good deal has been accomplished, and in this connection I would like to pay my respects to the late Chief Engineer of the Department of Public Works, who was out at the Pacific coast last year. It was my privilege on a number of occasions to confer with Mr. St. Laurent and I always found him very courteous, very much interested in his work, and more particularly did I find him very much interested in the problem of endeavouring to improve the Fraser river. I think that his death is a distinct loss to this country.
I would urge, upon the minister the advisability of continuing this work on the main channel of the Fraser river. I think that we have obtained results, and I am glad to see that the present minister is carrying on the work which was started by the previous administration, that he has taken hold and given this work a good deal of consideration. The business is there. What we require is a good safe and reliable channel so that our ships can take out our manufactured products to the various parts of the world. Our business is a very large one, and in that connection I might refer to the fact that the development of the Fraser river will mean something to tlris government, because the government owns something like four billion feet of standing timber in the Fraser river valley, which would pay dues to the Dominion when taken out. That timber is all in this district and is all available.
I should also like to refer to the fact that we have on the Fraser river sites for elevators. We have land already owned by the Dominion government or by the Canadian National railways at Port Mann, at New Westminster, and at Woodward's Landing, with water front suitable in all respects for the construction of elevators. If the government is going to build any elevators it will not be necessary for them to buy land any place else, they have it already on the Fraser river, and that land is already connected with their own railroads. If you establish elevators on the Fraser river you are going to assist the Canadian National railways because they have direct access to that land and sufficient trackage is available. The railway is already there. The Canadian National railways are already established at Port Mann. Perhaps that

Supply-Public Works
would be an ideal site for an elevator. At Woodward's Landing, if you wished to get lower down and closer to the mouth of the river, you have half a mile of water front, which is also connected up with a line of railway built by the Canadian National system, but which is not at present being operated. It would not require a large expenditure to put that railway into shape. If you have elevators on the Fraser river your operating expenses for unloading the grain would be considerably less than at any other place. I quite appreciate the fact that the minister is very familiar with conditions, and I would impress upon him the advisability of giving very serious consideration to the necessity of establishing at least one elevator on the Fraser river. But if the government are not going to enter into that business-and, of course, they may feel that should be left to private enterprise -then I would say that if the improvement of the Fraser river channel is attended to, private concerns will have available a great many miles of very desirable sites for elevators. I am looking forward to the day when we will not have simply one elevator on the Pacific coast but dozens of them. The development of trade towards that end is bound to come. The feasibility of the Pacific route has been demonstrated. It used to be thought at one time that the Panama canal could not be utilized, and that grain could not be shipped economically or safely from a Pacific port. However, that day is past and we know now, it has been established beyond question, that the Pacific route is a desirable and a profitable one, and that from an economic standpoint a very large proportion of the grain that is grown on the prairies could be shipped through Pacific ports. Now, I would say to the minister that the Fraser river is the place that this grain should be shipped from; I do not think there is any doubt in the world as to the desirable locations we would have if only our channel were placed in proper condition.
There is a point in connection with the sawmilling industry, which is not generally known and which I would like to mention. That is that fresh water is better adapted for the operation of sawmills than salt water, owing to this fact: In a salt water the logs will be badly affected by the teredo and damaged to a very considerable extent in a few months. That is not the case at all in fresh water. It has been proved by experience that sawmills should, wherever possible, be located on fresh water. Sawmill concerns are now taking advantage of that fact and are to a large extent removing their mills from salt water to
fresh water. That is where the importance of the Fraser river comes in.
There is another branch of the Fraser to which I would like to refer for a minute and that is the north arm. The minister knows the north arm very well. He has been over it several times and he has also, I think, been presented recently with a petition asking for some further improvement of the channel of the north arm. Now the north arm is a different proposition, inasmuch as we cannot expect within a reasonable time to have any great depth of water, but we may look forward to seeing industries located along that channel which require attention. Now, the minister has before him a petition dealing with this matter and I would urge upon him the necessity of giving that petition every consideration. I do not wish to take up time unnecessarily but, as I see it, the main channel and the north arm of the Fraser river provide a fresh water port for the peninsula upon which Vancouver and New Westminster are situated, and it is very necessary, if the future of that district is to be assured, that the channels in both cases should be improved. I hope the minister will continue the good work which he has been doing and that it will be proceeded with as rapidly as possible.

I do not intend to take up very much of the committee's time but I would draw the attention of the minister to the riding of Cariboo. Although that riding contains 165,000 square miles these estimates do not contain one dollar for the carrying out of improvements within its limits. Not only does the riding contain the area I have stated, but it also contains 1,500 miles of navigable waters in the shape of rivers, and indeed one lake has no less than 800 miles of shore line. Now I do not see why the minister has entirely ignored improvements for that immense district. I certainly think he should pay some attention to the Cariboo riding.
There are three matters that I would like to bring to his notice. First, Canoe wharf. This wharf has been recommended by the engineer for the last three or four years, the estimated cost of the work being $4,500. Before I came down here I went over the ground with the engineer and we agreed to cut the estimate down to $1,200. The wharf was built some eight or nine years ago, at a width of 16 feet and a length of 500 feet. When a team goes out to the end of the structure it has got to back out to the shore again, indeed, the wharf is practically useless in its present condition. The $1,200 in question would widen the wharf at the outer end so that
Supply-Public Works

teams could turn. I would ask the minister if he can see his way to including this improvement in the estimate of $75,000.
It could not be included in the present estimate.

Then I would ask whether
the minister could see his way to including the item in the Supplementary Estimates to be brought down later?
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I thought he was discussing "Fraser river improvements $75,000." My hon. friend, however, was discussing the general vote?

Yes. I would ask the
minister to see whether he cannot make provision for carrying out this work under the general vote.
The matter will be considered.

There is still another matter, in connection with Salmon Arm, to which I wish to draw attention. Last year the government voted $4,500 to improve the wharf there. That work was carried out very satisfactorily and the people of the locality appreciate it. However, there is a channel that was dredged out, I think about thirteen years ago, and owing to the dredge being dismantled some time during the war nothing has been done since to keep the channel clear. Now that channel needs-sto be dredged out, in fact the wharf is of very little use unless that dredging is done. I hope the minister will see his way clear to have that work carried out without delay.
I understand that the dredge is to be reconditioned, and it is the intention of the department to do some dredging on the lake this year.'

There is another item I want to bring to the attention of the minister, although possibly it may be out of order under this heading. In Kamloops there are some five buildings being rented by the government at a cost of $9,000 a year. A building could be erected for less than $100,000 which would accommodate all the departments now using the buildings referred to. I would like to know from the minister if he is prepared to recommend the carrying out of something along this line. Even if the outlay reached a total of $100,000 the money would not cost the government more than 6 per cent and there would still be a saving of $3,000 as compared with the cost under the present system of renting. Not only that,

but the employees concerned would be provided with far better accommodation than they now enjoy. The buildings now occupied are far from being fire proof, in fact, the post office at Kamloops has been twice condemned by the sanitary inspector there. For many reasons it is very important that the improvement which I have suggested should be carried out without delay. I would like to know from the minister if he will also give this matter his -consideration?

Before the minister replies I would like to take the opportunity of expressing, in common I know with others, the high appreciation I feel, and have always felt, of the services of Mr. St. Laurent who, unfortunately, has died lately. I came in contact with them very intimately, and over a long period of time. I was the means of having him appointed on the Dominion Power Board, and in other special matters of great engineering difficulty I availed myself of his services. I found him a man of high professional capacity, and as well, possessed of a keen sense of duty; to duty he devoted himself unceasingly throughout all the period of our acquaintance. I learned with the very deepest regret of the death of a servant of the public such as he, and I desire to record before this House my sense of our loss.

I am sure I can concur in every word that has been stated by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and the member for New Westminister. It was my good fortune as minister of the department to come closely in contact with the late Mr. St. Laurent while he was acting in the capacity of Chief Engineer of the Department of Public Works. As has been stated, he was a man not only of excellent engineering knowledge and ability, but of excellent parts and character, a very lovable man, and his loss is and will be greatly felt by the department and in government circles.
Will the minister give us a short statement of what he proposes to do on the Fraser river?

I have listened with great interest to my hon. friend's address on the requirements of the Fraser river, and the north arm of the Fraser. These are two important waterways in British Columbia and the Department of Public Works has tried to solve certain natural difficulties that exist there. During the flood season great quantities of alluvial material come down

Supply-Public Works
the Fraser and are deposited in the lower region, which results in the necessity of a very large expenditure being made from year to year in dredging and keeping the channel clear. Under carefully prepared plans, and after consultation and so on, the Department of Public Works, or the engineering board, did make certain recommendations. Last summer when going west I had the chief engineer the late Mr. St. Laurent accompany me, in order that he might have local knowledge of conditions for himself, and if possible concur in the recommendation of the engineering committee. He made that trip and spent considerable time on the Fraser river and did concur in the plans and suggestions made by the engineering com-mitee. That being so, we have let the contract for the construction of a retaining wall, amounting to something over $100,000, and this vote is for the purpose of taking care of that contract. It is hoped the construction of this wall will bring about a deepening of the channel and will also elminate the annual loss which now takes place through the filling up of the channel at that point.
What depth of water would that give us?

Thirty feet. In regard to the north channel, the department has from year to year carried on certain dredging operations, and at one time built a retaining wall at the mouth of the river. The matter of extending that wall further out to sea, or continuing our dredging operations, is now under consideration in the department.
I presume the minister refers, in connection with the extension of the wall, to the jetty on the north arm.
Yes.

Apparently the present
vote does not cover it, and my purpose in rising is to urge upon the minister and the government the expedience and the necessity of making that extension. With the presence of the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Fielding) I feel that my appeal is particularly strong, because if we cannot justify the request on the basis of business necessity then we would not ask for an appropriation for the extension of that jetty. In making this appeal to the government and the minister, which I hope will have their favourable consideration when the Supplementary Estimates come up, let me urge upon the minister the fact that I speak not only in behalf of private individuals, who favour this project, but I make the
appeal for the reeves, councillors and boards of trade of South Vancouver, Point Grey, Richmond, Burnaby and New Westminster, all of whom have met on two or three occa-' sions, coming from great distances to get together. They have given the matter consideration and are of the opinion that, both in the interests of preserving the channel on the north, and preventing filling by cross drifts at the mouth of the Fraser river, and in order to provide booming grounds for the large quantity of logs that are towed up the river, an extension of the jetty there is necessary. It is a business justification. At the present time the mouth of the north arm of the Fraser river fills in with silt caused by the cross currents in the river. There are two projects I believe under consideration, one being to clear the channel by dredging and the other to extend the jetty. I believe reports are being forwarded to the minister and that these reports are favourable-at least so I would judge-to the extension of the jetty. This is regarded as the least expensive method of preserving the investment the government has already made on the north arm, which investment exceeds $600,000. The extension will only cost, I believe, in the neighborhood of $40,000, and it will be a direct benefit to a very large number of industries. I would draw the attention of the government to the fact that there is a capital investment of $3,000,000 in the different industries along the Fraser river, which depend upon the channel of the north arm on which they carry on their business. There are four large shingle mills, having a daily output of 3,000,000 shingles, and six sawmills with a cut of 130,000 feet of lumber each day. They have 1,035 employees with a monthly payroll of over $22,000. There is not only the question of keeping the channel clear of the sand and silt that come in there so that the sawlogs and other traffic can be carried up the river but there is the equally important, and perhaps more important, question of the extension of this jetty in order to provide a booming ground there. At the present time the booms coming from the northern coast of British Columbia are brought down to a place called Howe Sound. They are brought down in large quantities, and at Howe Sound they are split up into smaller booms, and are brought down to the north arm of the Fraser to supply these mills. Sometimes they have to remain there for a considerable period before they can get up the river, or they have to be broken up into still smaller booms. The extension of the jetty is necessary, not only to protect the

channel, but to provide facilities so that these large booms which come down from the north can be taken to the north arm of the Fraser river, split up there into smaller booms and taken up the Fraser river. Competent men engaged in this industry state that there will be a saving of 50 cents per thousand on logs if the booms can be broken up at the mouth of the Fraser river. It is well known that a saving of 50 cents per thousand to the lumber and shingle mill industry in British Columbia would be of the very greatest advantage in competition with the many American mills just across the line, some few miles distant. Therefore, on behalf of the reeves, councillors and boards of trade of five large municipalities and cities, with some 75,000 of population, tributary to the north arm, who are asking for this improvement, I would strongly urge on the government the wisdom and necessity of including that in the Supplementary Estimates as it is not mentioned in the present appropriation.

Dredging-Maritime provinces, $600,000.
How much was spent last year?
All but $20,000.
What is the programme in the Maritime provinces for the coming year?

I presume this dredging is necessary, but those of us who live so far inland do not know why these large expenditures are required. Is it that the harbours are filling up with silt carried down by the rivers, or is the draught of the vessels increasing? Why has it been necessary last year and this vear to spend so large an amount as $600,000?'

The dredging is necessary chiefly because of silt coming down and filling up the harbours. There is a very long coast line, as my hon. friend knows. Where possible the department is constructing retaining walls to try and keep these deposits out.

Is this work to be done entirely by contract?

Supply-Public Works
It is departmental work largely.
Can the minister say how the money will be spent proportionately as between Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick?
I have not the information here in that form, but if my hon. friend desires it, I shall be very glad to advise him later.

The hon. member for Lisgar asked why it was necessary to repeat this expenditure from year to year. Now if he were down to the ifrovince of Nova Scotia and saw the Atlantic ocean throwing itself up against the rocks and upon the coast he would not wonder why it was necessary for. the minister of this or any other government to come and ask the House for an appropriation for this work. Often when the work has been done a storm will come up in the fall, or in the spring or winter months and beach rocks and stones and all sorts of debris will be thrown up and the work has to be done over again.
I rose particularly to call the minister's attention to the needs of the port of Windsor on the river Avon in the county of Hants. As my hon. friends all know, Windsor is one of the oldest ports in the Maritime provinces, standing near the mouth of the Avon river. This river is subjected to tremendous tides, and the dredging work which is done one year must of necessity be repeated next year in order to make navigation possible. Besides being one of the oldest ports in the Maritime provinces Windsor is, if not the third, at least the fourth most important port in the province of Nova Scotia, from the standpoint of shipping. We have great gypsum deposits there, and the Wentworth Gypsum Company of Windsor, the J. B. King Company of New York export annually about 200,000 tons of gypsum. WTe have also the Mosher quarries and other plaster companies using that port. It is also a great lumbering section, and the people have no other way except through the port of Windsor to get their stuff to market save over the railway, which costs a great deal of money by way of freight. There are many hundreds of thousands of feet of lumber to be shipped to the United States annually through that port, and it is necessary that it be put in proper shape to enable the shippers to get their gypsum and lumber and other products to the markets of the world. There is. also a great potato growing country, as well as a great apple growing country, adjoining the port, but to-day we are in such a position that it is impossible for us to get vessels to

come to that port owing to the unsatisfactory condition of the harbour. There is urgent need for dredging there.
It is all very well to follow the policy which has been followed in the past of getting some ten or fifteen men to shovel some of the mud away from around the docks, probably at a cost of $2,000 or $3,000 annually, but while that does some little good it is practically worthless work, as it is not nearly sufficient to enable the port to be a success. When the tide is out the vessels lie aground and it is necessary that the mud be shovelled up and taken away so that these vessels can lie at the docks. It is utterly impossible to charter a vessel to come to Windsor to-day without pas'ing a higher freight percentage than she will get for going to any of the other ports of Nova Scotia, and the result is that the trade of the town is becoming stagnant or is being taken to other places. We have been hampered through the condition of the harbour for a great number of years.
Windsor is the fourth most important port from the standpoint of customs receipts in the province of Nova Scotia, and in the old days it was one of the most wealthy ports of the province, and a great shipbuilding place. To-day some thirty or forty thousand people from the town and surrounding country are dependent on the port of Windsor for getting their goods to market. In 1914 we had public docks in the town of Windsor, but for some reason or other the government of the day leased these wharves to the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company, along with the railway to Windsor Junction for ninety-nine years at an annual rental of about $22,500 a year. Prior to that time there was an agreement whereby the wharves were held by the people, but the railway was leased on a basis of one-third of the gross receipts, and in 1913 the gross receipts were something like $43,000. In the year 1914, notwithstanding the fact that the receipts had reached the amount of $43,000, the railway took over this wharf and the railway for a term of ninety-nine years at an annual rental of $22,500. We have a very small wharf there, and we were told at the time of the lease that this would be extended and that considerable dredging would be done and the waterfront put in a proper state for shipping. But as a matter of fact we have a small wharf there to-day at which a vessel of 150 tons cannot lie, and she is a very small schooner, without the bowsprit projecting over the old government wharf, which is now in the hands of the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company, and the main boom extending over the Smith wharf on the other side. I would therefore ask

Supply-Public Works
the minister to consider well the needs of the port of Windsor and to put a substantial item in the estimates this year for dredging and a wharf at that port. It is all very well to say that we will allocate from this general vote two or three thousand dollars for dredging, but the port of Windsor needs from $50,000 to $60,000 for the improvement of the wharf and harbour and for dredging in order that the channel may be made safe and efficient, so that the port of Windsor shall take its rightful place in the province of Nova Scotia and be able to maintain its record. I believe that if we get adequate shipping facilities, Windsor will be at least the third most important shipping point in the province. If we had the adequate dock facilities we enjoyed in days gone by, there would be sufficient return from these wharves in wharfage charges to pay the interest on the capital expenditure. I therefore bespeak from the minister his most earnest attention to the needs of this port, which is one of the oldest in the Maritime provinces, and whose hardy people do need proper facilities to get their goods to market.

My hon. friend will agree that the development of art in any country is a great asset to the people-is, indeed, a matter of national importance. The National Gallery is serving a very useful purpose. It was reopened in September, 1921, and during the first year after its reopening it was visited by 106,000 people. The year ending March 31 will show an attendance of an equal number. The chief work of the National Gallery during the past year has been the maintenance and development of the national collection and the continuation of the loan exhibitions throughout Canada, of which eighteen have been held. The total amount appropriated by parliament since the establishment of the National Gallery Board in 1907 is $550,000. Making allowance for expenses and maintenance not more than $450,000 has been expended in works of art. The total value of the collection is conservatively estimated at current prices to be worth from $1,000,000 to $1,500,000, and in the opinion of competent judges it is one of the best collections on this continent. The trustees have made strong representations that they can secure from the Old Country to-day some very valuable pictures at a very reasonable cost.

I have visited the National Gallery and have seen some very nice pictures there. I think the collection we now have at the National Gallery is as good as we can afford at the present time. I think this vote should not be increased this year, and I am surprised that the Finance Minister has given it his sanction. I know how strong an advocate he is of economy, and when we are taxing the clothing and other necessaries of our people in order to raise the money on which to run this country I do not think it is right to vote an extra $50,000 for the purchase of more pictures. Pictures are nice things to look at, but they will not keep you warm nor fill an empty stomach, and I would move that this vote be reduced by the sum of $50,000.
Are these gentlemen going to the Old Country to purchase these pictures? Who purchases them?
The trustees serve without charge. I do not know of any charge that has been made in connection with trips to the Old Country.
Who are the trustees?

Sir Edmund
Walker, Toronto, Chairman; Dr. F. J. Shepherd, Montreal; J. Auguste Richard, Montreal; Newton McTavish, Toronto, and Warren Soper, Ottawa.
If I remember rightly, this is the former grant.

Yes.

Supply-Public Works
And it was diminished in what year?
And then to $50,000 later.
Yes.
These purchases are not confined entirely to Europe? Several are made in Canada, I understand?
Yes. They are trying to encourage Canadian art. There are many pictures by Canadian artists in the National Gallery.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are quite a number of items in the Estimates concerning which the same criticism might be offered as that which has just been made by my hon. friend (Mr. Coote). There are a great many items of which you could say: They do not keep you warm or do not feed people. But after all, there is something in the encouragement of art, and I do not think this is a very extravagant sum for us to vote. We must not be heartless, but we do not want to be artless, and I think the grant proposed, especially as it is simply a renewal of the former grant, is one that ought to commend itself to the House. We ought not to be too materialistic. Let us have a little admiration for the fine arts. If we do not appreciate them as much as we ought to, let us make good our defects by doing what we can for those who do appreciate them. I am not a connoisseur in the fine arts, but I would not like to see parliament reducing this item simply because it will not keep us warm or give us food.

I just want to say a word in defence of my action in moving this amendment. If the estimate had been left at $50,000, the same as last year, I would have offered no objection. I am not objecting to art at all. As I said before, I have visited the National Gallery and seen some very fine pictures there and enjoyed them, but I think we can get a good deal of enjoyment out of the pictures that are already there and out of what may possibly be purchased with the $50,000. Beyond that I do not think this committee ought to go at this particular time, when we have the Minister of Finance reminding us on every occasion that we must practise economy.

Notwithstanding what has been said by the Minister of Finance and the respect that I have both for him and the minister whose estimates we are now passing upon, I am entirely in sympathy with the
amendment. I cannot imagine any member of this House passing through the districts covering hundreds of miles of the prairie provinces and seeing the difficulties in which many of the farmers are, drawing their grain sixteen or seventeen or twenty miles, and they have been doing so for many years, seeing the children ill-clad because of the lack of the wherewithal, seeing the schools closed because they' cannot hire a teacher-I cannot imagine anyone who has seen these hardships who would think it wise or right to pass this item and expend the money for this purpose at this time. It may be thought that at times we are over-stating the case, and that we are, as the Finance Minister has said, too materialistic, but I assure you that the difference is this: We come from those districts. We have moved from home to home among these people and have seen the conditions, and that is the reason we have a greater sympathy for these people. While I do not wish to embarrass the government when they are doing what is right and wise I think it is for the reason I have given that the hon. member (Mr. Coote) has been moved to bring forward this amendment, and it is for that reason also that I must support it.

Before we vote on the amendment, I think I should give the committee the representations which the trustees, who, as I have already said, have undertaken this work for the people of Canada without any charge, have made to the government. This item was not placed in the estimates until they had come before the department and before the government and made their representations, and I think it is due to them that I should make them known to the committee:
As chairman of the trustees, National Gallery, I am authorized to apply for sum of $100,000 to be placed in the 1923-1924 Estimates on behalf of the National Gallery of Canada.
It is only natural that this work requires steadily increasing support on the part of the government if it is to be maintained and to progress in accord with the development of the culture and education of the country. In addition to maintaining the galleries at Ottawa, the National Gallery is conducting a very extensive campaign for the education of the country in a knowledge of the fine arts. During the past three years over fifty exhibitions of Canadian art have been held, and practically every city of importance from the Atlantic to the Pacific has been served in this way. In a great many communities the remarkable progress of art in recent years is almost entirely attributable to these exhibitions from the National Gallery, and in every case they have been the cause of great encouragement and permanent benefit.
In asking for the sum of $100,000 the trustees are fully cognizant of tbe necessity for economy and they are therefore only asking at the present time for a return to the appropriation received in the years 1913-
Supply-Public Works

14 and 1914-15 when the activity and importance of the National Gallery was comparatively limited to what it is now and when all works of art were cheaper. The trustees note that the government's grant to the Royal Canadian Academy has risen from $5,000 in 1914 and $2,500 during the war to $7,500. At such a scale of increase the National Gallery would be justified in asking for $150,000.
The trustees also wish to point out that owing to the unfavourable financial and other conditions in Europe at present, one hundred thousand dollars judiciously expended now will be of greater advantage than a much larger amount a few years hence when rare works of art will undoubtedly have still further increased in price or have become practically unobtainable.
I think that is all I wish to say. Undoubtedly the work is an important one. We have some very celebrated artists in Canada and the development of art will prove a benefit to the people of this country. I would be sorry to see the committee refuse this vote. *

I think I can appreciate the point of view of the hon. member who moved the amendment. I agree that there is much suffering and difficulty in the economic world but I do not think this is the best place to begin and correct it. Certainly I am not one who believes in the seemingly cynical popular idea of economy; I think that money well spent is the best kind of economy. Out of the hundreds of thousands of dollars we have voted in the last few days, I do not think money could be spent in a better way than is proposed here. I would not be surprised if this money brought greater benefit to the country than any of the other expenditures we have authorized.
Amendment (Mr. Coote) negatived.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa Parliament building-tablet to the memory of the late Bowman B. Law who lost his life in the fire which destroyed the old Parliament Building, $5,000.
Would the minister give us some information in respect to this item?	.

It is proposed to erect a tablet in the corridors of the building to commemorate the death of Mr. Bowman
B.	Law, member for Yarmouth, who was unfortunately caught in the building at the time of the fire and lost his life. A design for this tablet has been prepared and submitted to the trustees of the National Gallery and models have been invited, received, and referred to this committee.

This item, it seems to me, is on an altogether different basis from that to provide money for the purchase of paintings for the National Gallery. I know nothing about the gentleman to whom this tablet is to be erected. We have not been 
told that he has performed any great or special service to the country. I take it that the chief advantage in this would be that we are to have an ornamental tablet to further decorate the parliament buildings. It does seem to me that here is a case where we might well effect economy. All through the country there are many cases of estimable men who have lost their lives in various ways while engaged in carrying on the industrial work of this Dominion, and many monuments might be erected, from coast to coast, to the memory of such men. It seems to me that there is a danger that we are centralizing these things in these parliament buildings and I, for one, feel that only under exceptional circumstances should we spend money for such a purpose at this particular time.

Item agreed to.
Surveys and inspections, $110,000.
Where is this inspection taking place at the present time?

This vote is required to provide for any surveys or inspections that may be necessary during the fiscal year 1923-24 in connection with harbours, rivers, slides, booms and bridge work, and other services under the control of the Department of Public Works. It is a contingency item. A little while ago some of my hon. friends made inquiry regarding certain investigations made last year in connection with the flooded area in the Northwest. I imagine this expenditure would be connected with work of that character.
How much was spent last year?
The sum of $102,687 was expended last year.
I notice that an item above, amounting to $465,000 seems to include engineering equipment, surveys, etc.

The item my hon. friend refers to is to provide for the salaries of the regular staff. This vote is to meet inspection, travelling expenses, and expenditure of that kind in connection with extra work undertaken.

Item agreed to.
National monument on Connaught place, $10,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

The possibility of erecting a national monument on Connaught place which my hon. friend probably

Supply-Public Works
knows is the square located between the post office, Central Station and the Chateau Laurier, I understand has been under discussion for some years. It has been suggested that some form of national monument should be erected, and we are placing this amount in the estimates with a view to getting the matter under way. There have been several suggestions as to the character and form this monument should take. The whole matter is being considered carefully by a committee of council and the present item is placed in the estimates on their recommendation.
Is this a preliminary vote?
Yes, it is a preliminary vote.

I for one wish to object to this expenditure. It seems to me that this is also a matter which ought to require very careful consideration indeed before we embark on such expenditure. Men who served in the recent war are walking the streets to-day without work and their families are on the verge of starvation. I submit that we ought to fully provide for every one of these men before a cent is expended in the erection of a monument of stone.

I must
also express my objection to this item. I think it is a very unwise expenditure at this time.
I would like some further information respecting this matter. What form is the monument to take?

I do not think
that has yet been determined. I tried to make it plain to the committee that a committee of council are giving this matter consideration, with a view of developing something that would be suitable as a national monument. There have been several suggestions made, one being that we might have a monument in the capital city of the Dominion to commemorate confederation. Since the Great War it has been suggested that the efforts of the Canadian soldiers in France should be commemorated and that it would be a fit and appropriate thing to have a monument of that character in the capital city of Canada. There have been several suggestions. I think the desire of the Prime Minister was to put a small item in the estimates this year, in order that the matter might be given consideration, and that a monument that would commemorate some of the phases of Canada's history might be erected in the capital city of Canada.

What does the minister
hope to accomplish by an expenditure of $10,000? How will the money be spent to accomplish this object.

These matters
are usually arranged by the government advertising a competition. The artists will prepare designs and submit them in competition. These designs will be judged according to their merits, the successful competitor securing the contract for the final work. That will be the first step.

Is parliament to bear the
whole cost. In othen districts the cities have to contribute to any monument erected in those cities. It seems to me the city of Ottawa which is just about as rich as any other city in Canada should bear a part of the expense of the erection of the monument.
The hon. member does not know Ottawa.

It seems to me this is rather vague. There is no definite object apparently nor is there any concrete idea in this proposition, except that we should have a national monument? I think it is an excellent idea, provided there is some special reason for it, and the time is suitable. I would suggest to the minister that the time is hardly suitable. It is not a pressing matter. There is no urgency about it, because the minister cannot tell us what it is for. I think this is a fair case for delay. Let us have this monument some time, but I do not think this is the appropriate or suitable time. I think we should withhold that expenditure for a few years to come.

It seems to me that before
we pass this item we should have some idea from the minister as to what the total cost of the monument when finished is likely to be. Is it going to be $10,000 this'year, $100,000 next year, and $300,000 the following year? Before we can pass intelligently on this matter, we should have some idea as to the extent of the project.

I must apologize
for not having a better knowledge of this item. It was inserted at the request of a committee of the Cabinet who had been, giving considerable consideration to this matter. I would prefer to let the item stand for the present and bring it up at a later date, when further information might be given.
Item stands.
New Brunswick-St. John Quarantine Station Partridge island-repairs and improvements, $3,000.

Is that in reference to supply of water?
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the next item is.

Item agreed to.
St. John Quarantine Station-Partridge island water supply, $1,000.
Mr. MaeLAREN:	I would like some particulars in reference to the water supply. What improvement is being made in the supply?

This amount is
required for general repair to the pipe line conveying supply of water from the main land to Partridge island.

Item agreed to.	>
Maritime provinces generally-Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs, etc., $38,000.
What is the difference between this item and the others we have had? Why separate them? This amount of $38,000 is for the Maritime provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

This is a general vote to maintain the Dominion public buildings in the three Maritime provinces, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. It also includes the items that formerly were voted separately for the cities of Halifax and St. John. It is all included in the one item. The expenditure under this item is $25,268. The items vary from $1,568, down to $558. It is for repairs to the buildings which take place from time to time.

Item agreed to.
Montreal ordnance stores building, $26,000.
Is this a new building? or repairs to the old one?

This amount of $26,000 is required as a third payment on the purchase of Grant garage, No. 1 Hillside avenue, Westmount, as authorized by order in Council dated April 16th, 1921, which is being used to house the ordnance and barracks stores and garage service previously located in the Head building, which was given up on the expiration of the. lease May 1st, 1921. This is the third payment. The payments extend over ten years. The total price is $140,000.

Item agreed to.
Ontario-Kitchener-government's share of cost of local improvements, $1,750.36.
Why should the government pay for the local improvements?

This amount of $1,750.36 is provided for the payment to the

city of Kitchener of the government's share of the cost of asphalt pavement on Benton street in front of the Kitchener public buildings. The municipal council of the city of Kitchener, under authority of by-law No. 1616, passed on 16th May, 1921, constructed a concrete asphalt pavement on Benton street, between King and Alma streets. This pavement had a total frontage of 698 feet and the cost of it amounted to $7,745.11, of which the city paid $1,798 for street intersections, culverts, etc. The balance, viz., $5,947.11 is charged against the properties which have a frontage of 581 feet. The cost per foot frontage therefore amounted to ten decimal 236 dollars and as the government property has a frontage of 171 feet along the street, the government's share of the cost amounts to $1,750.36. In other words, government properties, like other properties, are paying for local improvements at Kitchener. That is the common practice.
Is that the practice in all other cities?
Yes, for local improvements.
I did not understand it in that way.

I am rising, not to object to this item, but to get a little information which will apply to some other items also. As I understand the matter from the information of the minister, the government, in the case of all public buildings, is liable for its share of municipal improvements according to frontage, but it is not liable for any other form of municipal taxation.
We do not pay any general taxes; but with the government consenting rve do pay for local improvements.
With the government consenting? How long has this practice been in vogue?
For about twenty-five years.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa printing bureau improvements, $1,000.
Is a new building not to be erected for the Printing bureau? If so, is it necessary to put any improvements on the old one?
This amount is the balance of a contract that was let for some improvements to the present building.

Item agreed to.

Ottawa-towards purchase of Daly building, $148,000.
What is the explanation of this item?

This is to provide for payment of the third instalment of the purchase price of $1,000,000 for the Daly building. This building was leased to the government at an annual rental of $85,000. The owners of the building offered to sell it for $1,000,000, payable in ten annual instalments of $100,000 each with interest at 6 per cent. This is the third instalment, and there will be seven more payments.
When was the first payment made?
August, 1921.
What was the original cost of the Daly building? It seems to me that $1,000,000 for that kind of a building is out of all proportion to the cost.

This building was not constructed by the government. This is a purchase, and the chief architect of the department, in a memorandum
10 p.m. dated May, 1921, recommended the purchase of this building on the above-mentioned basis of $100,000 a year with interest at 6 per cent; spread over a period of ten years, as such a purchase was manifestly to the advantage of the Dominion government, if we regard it only from a rental basis, but a further consideration of this renders it desirable also as a rounding out of the property already purchased by the Crown.
How much will it cost to put this building into shape for government offices?

We were in occupation of the building under a rental costing $85,000 a year, and it was apparently considered advisable at that time to purchase the building, extending the payments over a period of ten years.

Item agreed to.
Saskatchewan-Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs, etc., $17,000.

Last spring I brought to the attention of the minister the post office facilities at Swift Current. I understand some years ago that the government bought certain ground in order later on to build a post office. Last year, when I was speaking to the minister, he said that he intended to look over the situation. Has he looked over the situation and if so, what conclusion has
Supply-Public Works
he reached? Is there in this appropriation any money for a post office at Swift Current?
We have made some inquiries, and we have entered into a new lease at a reduced rental for a term of one year for the property that we are now occupying.
Does the minister consider the present building suitable for a post office at Swift Current at the present time?
Our reports are that it is suitable.

Item agreed to.
Moose Jaw public building-improvements to heating, $12,000.
What does this comprise?

This is to provide for the installation of new boilers to replace the five existing boilers which are in poor condition and which cannot adequately heat the building, and also for the installation of
2,000	square feet of additional radiation which is necessary in order to maintain a temperature of 70 degrees inside the building during zero weather. It is asked for by the chief architect and requested by the mechanical engineer for the western provinces.

I think I asked, under the former vote of last year of $17,000, where the money was intended to be spent, and I think the minister said last year that a certain amount of this $17,000 was to be spent at Swift Current. How much of it was spent at Swift Current last year?

Last year, $880. Item agreed to.
Alberta-Calgary-customs examining warehouse-local improvement taxes, $3,737.10.
Is this a rented building and so subject to general taxation?
It is a government owned building.
The explanation given in regard to the last item applies to this?
Yes.

There is some discussion as to the general taxation that can be levied by municipalities on public lands or properties. The general principle is that no taxes can be levied on the Crown in that respect, and sometimes, of course, it works a great hardship on the municipalities. It struck me that, in the matter of taxation, pavements
Supply-Public Works

fronting government buildings would almost come under the same class as roads fronting government lands or properties. Is this item arrived at by arrangement between the government and the municipality concerned?
Improvements on the sidewalk leading to government property is a fair charge against that property. The matter is one of consent on the part of the government.
I was not objecting to the item. I was simply referring to the application of the principle and as to how far it extended.

Item agreed to.
Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs, etc.. $17,000.

I want to make a few remarks with regard to the Calgary post office. The Calgary post office, as a matter of fact, is something that does not exist. I quite understand that the matter has been under consideration by the government, for representations have Joeen made, I believe, on numerous occasions by the people of Calgary, through the mayor and council and other public bodies, requesting attention to that post office. The minister, no doubt, is aware that the Calgary post office was pulled down by a previous government, that, I believe, of Sir Robert Borden, the intention having been to prepare the way for a better and more commodious building. For some reason or other it was found advisable, it seems, not to carry on the work, and since then we have been looking at a huge hole in the ground instead of a post office. Before the government pulled it down the post office was giving reasonable service, and the city of Calgary has a reasonable and urgent claim upon the government at this time for a new building. The government is paying $50,000 or so annually for the rental of public buildings, all of which could be saved if a post office building were put up. This unseemly hole that is left in the ground now is a disgrace to the city and perhaps a greater disgrace to the government that made the hole. The building of a new post office has been urged by the city coim-cil, organized labour, and other public bodies, and I should like to know whether the minister intends making any provision for the work this year. It is badly needed; the people want it; and the appropriations for our province are comparatively small. Besides this, t{ie building of a post office at this time would materially relieve unemployment.

We are well advised as to the necessity of a public post office 
at Calgary, but to construct a building suitable for the district would mean a veiy large expenditure at this time, and it is not the intention of the government to proceed with the work this year.

Item agreed to.
British Columbia-Bamfield-public building, $1,500.
What is this for?
This is for work in connection with the public building at Bamfield, which is situated on the west coast of Vancouver island where there is a cable station.

Item agreed to.
Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs etc., $35,000.
What are the details of this item?

This is required for improvements, renewals and repairs in connection with the maintenance of public buildings in British Columbia, including those in the city of V ancouver for which previously a special appropriation was taken. This year, up to January 31st, we have spent $33,595. It is the usual maintenance vote.

Item agreed to.
Victoria-Old Post Office-taxes due city for 1922, $1,482.62.

An explanation was given of this vote last year, but the committee may have forgotten it. This is an old public building in the city of Victoria which the government have been renting, and for that reason, it being in competition with other property, for many years a tax has been paid on it as on other property. The government are now going to use the property for their own purposes, and once it reverts to that position we shall not pay taxes.

Item agreed to.
Armouries-fittings and alterations, $37,000.
What is this appropriation for?

This is required for fitting up rented buildings throughout the country for use as armouries as requested by the Deputy Minister of National Defence in a letter dated November 27th, 1922, in which he states that this estimate represents the minimum amount required by the department for repairs and alterations to non-permanent active militia headquarters, and it is

Supply-Public Works
therefore requested that the amount be included in the estimates for the fiscal year 1923-1924.

Item agreed to.
Dominion public buildings generally, $30,000.
* Mr. KING (Kootenay): This includes travelling expenses, stationery, drawings, instruments, etc. The appropriation for 1921-22 was $30,000; the expenditure was $29,767. This year our expenditure to January 31, was $18,775, leaving a balance unexpended of $11,000.
Item agreed to.
Dominion public buildings-power for running elevators, stamp cancelling machines, etc., $76,000.
Will the minister give the reason for the increase there?

The increase is accounted for by an appropriation of $5,292 due to transfer of an amount formerly paid out of another vote, together with an increase of $743 in the allotment for contingencies. These two items amount to $6,035, but there are a few slight decreases throughout the Dominion which reduce the total to $6,000.
How much of the vote for Dominion public buildings, which totals $5,135,500, is to be spent in Ottawa?
AH the items un- . der the heading "Ottawa public buildings" relate to Ottawa services. The others are for buildings outside Ottawa.

Item agreed to.
Dominion public buildings-rents, $1,450,000.
Will the minister please explain that? There is a big increase there.

The increase is due to provision being made for the rental of premises for the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the Soldier Settlement Board, for which no provision was made in the estimates of 1922-23, and which were formerly charged to demobilization vote; and to increases in rentals and new rentals entered into in 1922-23. Under Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment we have rentals of $115,000; Soldier Settlement Board, $43,582; increase in rentals, $31,486; new rentals, $46,322.
Is any portion of that for the city of Ottawa?
No.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 10.19 p.m.
